anomaly_def.Name: Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly + Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly
anomaly_def.Description:
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly: Engine-level runtime settings (memory, checkpoint, logging, parallelism, etc.) are mis-tuned relative to hardware capacity, workload characteristics, or version defaults, leading the database to behave inefficiently even when the physical resources themselves are not yet exhausted.
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly: On-disk table and index pages have become physically or logically corrupt—checksums, page links, key ordering, or heap-to-index mappings are inconsistent—making access paths and data validity unreliable.
Storage I/O Throughput Anomaly: The underlying storage subsystem is saturated in bandwidth, IOPS, or latency so that read/write requests queue up, inflating device wait times and slowing foreground and background database activity.

When all three anomalies co-exist, the system exhibits blended and mutually amplifying symptoms: chronic I/O waits and checkpoint storms despite moderate CPU usage; erratic query plans that oscillate between slow full scans (triggered by unusable or mistrusted indexes) and inefficient parallel plans driven by mis-set parameters; sudden surges in log-flush or buffer-flush waits followed by corruption warnings or checksum failures; extended recovery or backup windows impeded both by storage slowdowns and by pages that must be reread or repaired; divergent row counts between index and heap that cause application-level inconsistencies, all while traditional resource dashboards show puzzling mismatches between utilization and wait events.

Causally, misaligned configuration parameters (e.g., undersized buffer pools, overly aggressive checkpoint targets, or excessive parallelism) inflate the I/O demand placed on an already bandwidth-constrained storage layer, pushing it into sustained saturation. Prolonged high queue depths and latency increase the window in which partially written pages or logs remain vulnerable to power loss or crash scenarios, raising the likelihood of physical or logical page corruption. Conversely, existing block or index corruption forces the optimizer to abandon efficient access paths, switching to heavier scans that further strain the mis-tuned buffer and I/O subsystems. The feedback loop between excessive I/O pressure (from poor configuration and corruption-induced full scans) and storage throughput limits accelerates wear on the device, magnifies latency spikes, and complicates recovery, resulting in a severely degraded and unstable database environment where each root cause masks and intensifies the others.

entry.cause_analysis: The failure is typically associated with a general engine-level execution problem surfaced by the official error catalogue, but its precise trigger must be interpreted together with workload context and surrounding evidence.
entry.solution_guidance: Review the surrounding workload, official description, and engine state to determine whether the issue is rooted in SQL logic, resource pressure, configuration, or environmental instability.
